name: Stortok
description: Stortok (Swedish: 'Big Fool') is a Swedish card game related to the Russian game Durak. The primary goal is to get rid of all your cards. The winner is the first player out, and the last player holding cards is the 'Stortok' (Fool). It features attacking and defending mechanics, but with fewer complex card interactions than Durak.

content.text: Stortok (Swedish: 'Big Fool') is a Swedish card game related to the Russian game Durak. The primary goal is to get rid of all your cards. The winner is the first player out, and the last player holding cards is the 'Stortok' (Fool). It features attacking and defending mechanics, but with fewer complex card interactions than Durak.

Stortok is known from three documented sources: Lindskog (1847), Öberg (1858), and Schenkmanis (1980s, also in Norwegian as Kjempetosk). It is a Swedish beating game related to Durak, with two trump suits (high and low by colour). The 1847 and 1858 accounts differ from the late 20th-century version in deal size, trick structure, and lead rules.
Two to five players. The game is for 2 to 5 players; deal and play are clockwise.
36-card pack: from a standard 52-card pack remove the cards below 6; ranks A (high) down to 6 (low) in each suit.
36-card pack: from a standard 52-card pack remove the cards below 6; ranks A (high) down to 6 (low) in each suit.
Deal 5 cards to each player. Top card of remaining deck turned for Trump. Remainder forms Talon.

items.text: 1847 (Lindskog): 36 cards, 5 each, stock with turned trump; two trump suits (high and low by colour). Play pile; beat or pick up; draw after each play while stock has cards.
1858 (Öberg): Full 52-card deck; all cards dealt; last card dealt face up determines high trump. No stock; play continues until one player has all cards (the Stortok).

20th century (Schenkmanis): 36 cards, 5 each; turned trump may start first trick. Only the top card of the pile is picked up when failing to beat; completed tricks set aside; different lead after pick-up.
